headline: Robots That Choose, Bricks from Moon Dust and a Trade Bigger Than We Knew
teaser: Should machines ever decide who lives or dies? Can Moon dust become a home? And how many wild species are we really buying and selling?

articles.title: Nations Agree to Start Drafting Rules for "Killer Robots"
articles.dek: Governments have agreed to work toward rules for weapons that can pick their own targets, but is a slow deal that includes everyone better than a fast one that leaves out the biggest powers?
paras: After more than a decade of slow and often frustrating discussion, governments meeting in Geneva have taken what supporters call a significant step toward controlling weapons that can choose and attack targets without a human pulling the trigger. On 21 November 2026, the 128 countries at a United Nations arms-control conference agreed to spend the next two years working out a possible international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, often nicknamed "killer robots." The decision, however, was a compromise, and many campaigners left the talks disappointed rather than relieved.

The meeting took place under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), a treaty adopted in 1980 to restrict weapons considered excessively injurious or indiscriminate. Over the years, the convention has produced protocols on landmines and incendiary weapons, and in 1995 it banned blinding laser weapons before they were ever widely deployed. Many diplomats hoped autonomous weapons could follow the same path and be regulated early, before they spread. Informal talks on the subject began in 2014, but progress has been held back by one feature of the convention: its decisions require the agreement of every member state.

That rule shaped the final text. Nearly 100 countries had pushed for the swift adoption of legally binding rules, but key arms-producing states, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. According to diplomats, Russian objections over procedure led to some formal sessions being called off, and negotiators argued over wording through the night. Some delegations refused to accept the word "negotiate," so the agreed text speaks only of the "elaboration" of an instrument. To an outsider the difference may look trivial, yet in diplomacy it matters: negotiating implies an agreed destination, whereas elaborating commits no one to signing anything.

The chair of the conference, Swiss diplomat Julien Thoeni, nevertheless presented the outcome as evidence that cooperation is still possible. He said the result showed that "even in today's deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results." Under the plan, the process should determine which weapons could be banned outright under international humanitarian law, the body of rules that protects civilians in war, and which could be permitted but regulated. This two-tier approach is designed to attract states that reject a total ban but accept that some limits are needed.

Campaigners were far less impressed. Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of some 300 organizations, described the mandate as "watered down" and warned that it offers no clear route to binding law. Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, argued that "delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk," pointing out that autonomous systems, including ones that use artificial intelligence to select targets, are already being used in combat. Verity Coyle of Human Rights Watch put the problem more bluntly: the agreement "does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules – but the technology is racing ahead."

Behind the procedural dispute lies a deeper disagreement about whether machines should ever make life-and-death decisions. Opponents of autonomous weapons raise what they call the accountability gap: if an algorithm wrongly identifies a civilian truck as a military vehicle, it is unclear whether the programmer, the commander or the manufacturer should be held responsible. They also doubt that software can apply the core principles of the laws of war, such as distinguishing soldiers from civilians and judging whether an attack is proportionate. Some fear, too, that wars fought by machines could become easier to start, because fewer of a country's own soldiers would be at risk.

Defenders of the technology, and of a slower approach, see things differently. They argue that well-designed systems may react faster than people and could even make fewer mistakes than exhausted or frightened soldiers. Several major military powers also maintain that existing international humanitarian law already applies to every weapon, so a new treaty is unnecessary, and that premature rules could freeze a technology that is still evolving. From this perspective, a careful process involving every major power is better than a quick treaty that the countries building these weapons refuse to join.

Whether the next two years produce a meaningful agreement will depend largely on those reluctant states. A treaty signed only by countries that have no intention of building autonomous weapons would carry symbolic weight but little practical force. On the other hand, history shows that norms can spread even without universal support: the landmine ban of 1997 was negotiated outside the CCW and gradually changed behavior, even among some countries that never signed it. For now, the question is no longer whether rules are needed, but whether diplomats can write them before the technology outpaces them.

speak.p: Some people believe that machines should never be allowed to make life-and-death decisions, even if they make fewer mistakes than humans. Others think that if a machine is more accurate, it should be used. Which view do you agree with, and why?
speak.hint: Pick one side; give two reasons (e.g., responsibility, accuracy, fairness) and one example from the article; end with a one-sentence conclusion.

write.p:
Dr. Rivera: This week, 128 countries agreed to spend two years working toward rules on "killer robots", weapons that can select targets without a human decision. Because every member must agree, the deal is weak, and some countries building these weapons oppose a treaty. Is it better to wait for an agreement that includes every major power, or to move quickly with a treaty signed only by willing countries? Why?
Sophia: "We should move quickly. Every year of delay lets the technology spread further. A strong treaty signed by many countries creates pressure, just as the landmine ban did."
Daniel: "I disagree. A treaty without the countries that actually build these weapons is mostly symbolic. It is better to keep everyone at the table, even if progress is slow."
steps: Respond to Sophia or Daniel and add a new reason.
Support your view with an example, such as the landmine ban.
Finish with a short concluding sentence.

articles.title: Scientists Turn Moon Dust into LEGO-Like Bricks
articles.dek: Engineers have fused simulated lunar dust into small interlocking blocks without any glue from Earth, but is this a real step toward Moon bases or just a clever laboratory trick?
paras: When astronauts return to the Moon in the coming years, they will face a problem familiar to anyone who has ever moved to a new home: everything they need must be carried there, and carrying is expensive. Every kilogram of equipment launched from Earth adds enormously to the cost of a mission, so space agencies are keen to find ways of building with materials that are already on the Moon. A new study from the University of Arkansas, published in the journal npj Advanced Manufacturing, suggests that lunar dust itself could one day be turned into small, interlocking building blocks.

The idea of using local resources, known as in-situ resource utilization, is not new. Engineers have long imagined extracting water from lunar ice, oxygen from lunar rock and construction material from regolith, the layer of loose dust and broken rock that covers the Moon's surface. Regolith is abundant, but it is also an awkward material. Because the Moon has no wind or flowing water to wear particles down, its grains remain sharp and irregular, and they contain no organic matter that might help them stick together.

Earlier attempts to 3D-print with regolith typically mixed the dust with a binder, a glue-like substance that holds the particles together. The drawback is obvious: the binder itself would have to be transported from Earth, which undermines the whole point of using local material. The Arkansas team, led by Cole McCallum, who carried out the work as an undergraduate, and his supervisor, assistant professor of mechanical engineering Wan Shou, set out to remove the binder altogether.

To do so, they used a technique called laser powder bed fusion. A thin layer of powder is spread across a platform, and a concentrated beam of light fuses the particles where a solid part is needed. The platform then lowers slightly, a fresh layer is added, and the process repeats until a three-dimensional object emerges. Because real Moon dust is scarce and precious, the researchers worked with a commercially available simulant designed to resemble samples brought back by the Apollo missions. "There's nothing else it's binding to," McCallum explained. "The regolith powder is binding to itself."

The result was a set of small blocks, only a few centimeters across, shaped like crosses and the letter H. Like toy construction bricks, they can be slotted together and taken apart again, so a single set of pieces could, in principle, be reconfigured into different structures as a settlement's needs change. According to the researchers, this is the first time a regolith simulant has been fused directly into interlocking, reconfigurable blocks without any binder.

Yet the team is candid about the limitations. Compared with parts printed using binders, the binder-free blocks contain more internal pores and are structurally weaker. "These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum said, but he added that he "would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet." Nor does anyone yet know how the process will behave in the Moon's low gravity and near-vacuum, conditions that are very difficult to reproduce in a laboratory on Earth. Shou has said that improving the blocks' strength and durability is the next priority.

Not everyone is convinced that such bricks represent the most practical route to a lunar base. Skeptics point out that powerful lasers demand a reliable energy supply, which is itself scarce on the Moon, and that printing a whole habitat one small block at a time could be painfully slow. Some engineers favor simpler approaches, such as shipping inflatable or prefabricated modules and then covering them with loose regolith to shield astronauts from radiation. Supporters reply that every technology looks impractical at first, and that reconfigurable blocks could prove valuable for smaller tasks, such as building walls, landing pads or replacement parts.

Ultimately, the study is best seen as an early proof of concept rather than a finished solution. It shows that lunar dust can be persuaded to bond to itself, but turning palm-sized pieces into safe, load-bearing buildings will require years of further testing. Still, if humans are ever to live on the Moon for long periods, they will need to make far more of what they use from what they find there, and research like this is a small but meaningful step in that direction.

write.p:
Dr. Chen: Engineers have used lasers to turn simulated Moon dust into small interlocking blocks without any glue from Earth. The blocks are still weak, and no one knows how the process will work on the Moon. Should universities and governments fund early-stage research like this, even when practical results may be many years away? Why or why not?
Lucas: "Yes. Almost every major technology started as a small experiment. If we only fund research that already works, we will never discover anything new."

articles.title: The Wildlife Trade Is Far Bigger Than Anyone Thought
articles.dek: A new count finds almost 80,000 species in international trade, most of it legal and poorly recorded, so who should be responsible for tracking it: governments, companies or shoppers?
paras: From aquarium fish and potted orchids to timber, medicinal plants and exotic pets, wild species pass through human hands on a vast scale. Until now, scientists believed that roughly 50,000 species were involved in international trade. A new study published in Science Advances suggests that figure was a serious underestimate. Led by Alice Hughes of the University of Melbourne, with co-authors from organizations including TRAFFIC, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the research identifies 79,554 species in international trade, and the true number is probably higher still.

To reach this figure, the team combined information from a wide range of sources: the trade database of CITES, the international treaty that has regulated trade in protected species since 1975; the IUCN Red List of threatened species; United Nations records on fish and timber; seizure reports collected by TRAFFIC; and import records from the United States. They also searched for national wildlife-trade databases in 30 languages across 61 countries. When subsistence and other local uses were added, the total rose to 107,356 species, of which 47,685 were animals and 59,671 were plants and fungi.

Some of the individual findings are striking. Up to 31,306 vertebrate species, about 42 percent of all described vertebrates, have been traded. Around 65 percent of living bird species and roughly 37 percent of reptile species appear in trade, yet CITES covers only about 9.5 percent of reptile species. Where population data exist, the researchers found that wild populations from which animals are collected are, on average, 50 to 60 percent smaller than populations that are left alone.

The financial stakes are equally large. Legal wildlife trade is estimated to be worth between 220 and 300 billion US dollars a year, while illegal trade is thought to be worth 28 to 40 billion dollars. In other words, the legal market is roughly six to eleven times bigger than the black market that tends to attract headlines. This does not mean that the illegal trade is unimportant, nor that the legal trade is harmless. The lesson, rather, is that a trade this large, if it is poorly recorded, can drain wild populations without anyone noticing.

Poor recording is, in fact, the study's central concern. Almost no country systematically records what it buys and sells. "The United States is the only country that systematically records and publicly shares trade data across a wide range of taxa," Hughes noted. As a result, more than a quarter of traded animal species, and 54 percent of traded mammals, appear only in US records. Online sales make matters worse, because parcels sent by post are often not identified to the species level at the border. Even seizure data are imperfect, since they reflect how hard officials are looking as much as how much smuggling actually occurs.

The researchers argue that this gap matters for global conservation goals. The current global biodiversity framework includes a target on trade, but its main measure, the share of fish stocks harvested at sustainable levels, reflects only a tiny fraction of the species in trade. According to Hughes, it "misses the other 97 percent." Without better data on other groups, she argues, the trade simply "can't be managed."

Their proposed solutions are practical rather than dramatic. Instead of creating new institutions, they suggest standardizing how trade data are collected, starting at a regional level, possibly with the European Union as a first model. Since almost every country already carries out customs and animal-health checks on imports, shipping invoices could be digitized and matched against a list of species. Critics might respond that such systems are costly for poorer countries, and that traders could simply mislabel shipments. Supporters, however, note that similar tracking already works for livestock: in the United Kingdom, for example, sheep have been required to carry electronic tags since 2009.

Finally, the study turns attention to consumers. Pets, plants and wildlife products are bought by ordinary people, often without any idea of where they come from. "Almost all of us are part of wildlife trade," Hughes observed, and her advice is simple: if you are not sure where a product comes from, do not buy it. Not everyone agrees that individual choices can solve a global problem, since governments and large companies control most of the trade. Yet better information, for officials and shoppers alike, seems a necessary first step toward ensuring that the wild species we use today are still around tomorrow.

speak.p: Some people believe that protecting wild species depends mainly on governments and strict laws. Others think that ordinary consumers can make the biggest difference through what they choose to buy. Which view do you agree with, and why?
speak.hint: Choose one side; give two reasons and one example from the article (e.g., US trade records or Hughes's advice); end with a one-sentence conclusion.

write.p:
Dr. Patel: A new study finds that almost 80,000 species are traded internationally, and most of this trade is legal but poorly recorded. The authors call for better data and urge consumers not to buy products of unknown origin. Who should take the main responsibility for making the wildlife trade sustainable: governments or individual consumers? Why?
Olivia: "Governments. Only they can make countries record trade data and check shipments at the border. Individual shoppers cannot see where a fish or plant really came from."
Ethan: "Consumers matter more. If people stop buying exotic pets and products with unclear origins, companies will change their supply chains quickly, much faster than new laws are passed."
steps: State who should take the main responsibility.
Respond to Olivia or Ethan and add a new reason.
Support your view with a detail from the study.
End with a short concluding sentence.
